related_questions.question: What is a vaccine associated sarcoma?
related_questions.snippet: A vaccine-associated sarcoma (VAS) or feline injection-site sarcoma (FISS) is a type of malignant tumor found in cats (and, often, dogs and ferrets) which has been linked to certain vaccines. VAS has become a concern for veterinarians and cat owners alike and has resulted in changes in recommended vaccine protocols.

related_questions.question: What species has a higher rate of vaccine-associated sarcomas?

text_blocks.snippet: Cats have a significantly higher rate of vaccine-associated sarcomas compared to other species. While these tumors can occur in other animals, they are most frequently observed in cats, particularly at vaccination sites. The condition is so strongly associated with cats that it's often referred to as "feline injection-site sarcoma" by the American Veterinary Medical Association.
Here's why cats are more susceptible:

list.title: Increased susceptibility to inflammation:
list.snippet: Some studies suggest cats have a greater susceptibility to oxidative injury and inflammatory responses, which are believed to play a role in the development of these sarcomas.

list.title: Specific vaccine types:
list.snippet: Rabies and Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) vaccines, particularly those containing adjuvants, have been most commonly implicated, according to the Veterinary Information Network®, Inc. - VIN.

list.title: Multiple vaccinations at the same site:
list.snippet: Repeated vaccinations in the same location can increase the risk of sarcoma development.

list.title: Slow tumor growth:
list.snippet: The tumors can take months or even years to appear after vaccination, making it challenging to establish a direct link.
